changelog.change: Initial entry — Donaldson grading, mechanism, risk factors, the shared surgical/anaesthetic prevention checklist, and grade-by-grade management (RV-failure framing). From the CV BCIS audit + the primary Donaldson 2009 review and the 2015 AAGBI hemiarthroplasty safety guideline.

summary: Hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia, or arrest occurring around femoral canal pressurisation, prosthesis insertion, or joint reduction during a cemented arthroplasty — an embolic shower (fat, marrow, cement, air, debris) causing pulmonary vascular obstruction and acute right-heart strain, with a monomer-mediated vasodilatory component. Grade by the Donaldson scale, treat it as right ventricular failure, and stop cementing.
whyThisMatters: The highest-incidence setting is a cemented hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture in an elderly patient with limited cardiopulmonary reserve — exactly the population least able to tolerate an acute rise in pulmonary vascular resistance — and the deterioration lands in a predictable 30-60 second window that the anaesthetist can be ready for. Severe BCIS (grade 2-3) carries real perioperative mortality, and a hypovolaemic patient at the moment of cementation is the setup that turns a transient dip into an arrest.
clinicalTakeaway: Anticipate it: before cementation, raise FiO2 toward 1.0, confirm euvolaemia, have a vasopressor drawn up and running low-dose if needed, and make sure the surgeon announces cementation. If BCIS occurs — 100% oxygen, IV fluids, an alpha-agonist (phenylephrine) first, escalate to noradrenaline then adrenaline for RV failure or refractory hypotension, hold further cementation, and run ACLS for grade 3. Treat it as acute RV failure: support coronary perfusion pressure, avoid fluid overload and further increases in PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis), and consider an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (epoprostenol / nitric oxide) if there is a pulmonary-hypertensive crisis. Most survivors are transient — but monitor for delayed hypoxia and embolic complications.

rows: Moderate hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) OR hypotension (fall in systolic BP > 20%)
Severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%) OR hypotension (fall in systolic BP > 40%) OR unexpected loss of consciousness

body.text: Grade 1 is common and usually self-limiting; grades 2-3 are the ones with a mortality signal. The event typically begins within 30-60 seconds of cement or prosthesis insertion (or of reduction / tourniquet release in a cemented knee) and evolves over a few minutes.

items: Canal pressurisation drives an embolic shower — fat, marrow, cement particles, air, and bone debris — into the pulmonary circulation, causing mechanical obstruction, an increase in pulmonary vascular resistance, and acute right ventricular strain / failure.
Mediator release (thromboxane, complement, tissue factor) amplifies pulmonary vasoconstriction and can trigger arrhythmia.
Methylmethacrylate monomer absorption contributes a direct systemic vasodilatory / negative-inotropic effect, worse in a hypovolaemic patient.
Net picture: acute cor pulmonale — low cardiac output from a pressure-overloaded RV, systemic hypotension, hypoxia from V/Q mismatch and a low mixed-venous saturation.

Patient: age > 75-80, ASA 3-4, pre-existing pulmonary hypertension or significant cardiopulmonary disease, osteoporosis, bony metastases / pathological fracture, and a hip FRACTURE (vs an elective arthroplasty).
Surgical: a cemented (vs uncemented) femoral component, a long-stem femoral prosthesis, a first-time procedure (vs revision), and aggressive canal pressurisation.
Setting: cemented hemiarthroplasty for femoral neck fracture has the highest reported incidence; also cemented TKA (at tourniquet release), vertebroplasty / kyphoplasty.

Surgeon: thorough canal lavage, brushing and drying; retrograde cement application with a cement gun and a suction/vent catheter; minimise the pressure and duration of pressurisation; be cautious with long stems and pathological bone; consider an uncemented or modern-cementing technique in the highest-risk patient.

Anaesthetist: correct hypovolaemia BEFORE cementation; increase FiO2 toward 1.0 just before cement; have phenylephrine / ephedrine drawn up and noradrenaline available, and start a low-dose infusion pre-emptively in a marginal patient; maintain normocarbia, normothermia, and normal pH (all raise PVR when deranged).
Team: an explicit verbal 'cementing now' call so monitoring attention and vasopressor readiness are synchronised to the event.
Corticosteroid pre-treatment (e.g. methylprednisolone) has one small positive trial and is reasonable in a very high-risk case, but is not established practice; dexamethasone alone is untested.
Grade 1: FiO2 1.0, a fluid bolus, and a bolus alpha-agonist (phenylephrine 50-100 mcg) — usually enough. Inform the surgeon; reassess before any further cement.

Grade 2: as above plus a vasopressor infusion (noradrenaline), consider adrenaline for RV support / low output, invasive arterial monitoring, and hold further cementation. Get a blood gas; treat hypoxia, hypercarbia, and acidosis aggressively because each raises PVR further.
Grade 3: ACLS. Adrenaline, chest compressions, secure the airway, and treat the reversible cause — this is obstructive shock from acute cor pulmonale. Abort further cementation.

RV-failure principles throughout: maintain systemic (coronary) perfusion pressure with a vasopressor, avoid volume overload of the failing RV, minimise anything that raises PVR, and consider an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (epoprostenol or nitric oxide) and TOE if a pulmonary-hypertensive crisis is suspected. VA-ECMO is a salvage option in a refractory grade-3 event in a candidate.
After stabilisation: most events are transient. Continue high FiO2, monitor for delayed hypoxaemia and further embolic phenomena (fat embolism syndrome, PE), and consider ICU admission for grade 2-3.
